docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Several examples are available in the examples folder of the repository to exploit the functionalities related to:

  • exhausted modes (M) and the fast/active/slow subspaces;
  • tangential stretching rate (TSR);
  • CSP and TSR indices (importance indices, amplitude and timescale participation indices, TSR amplitude/timescale participation indices);
  • CSP solver and G-Scheme;
  • CSP simplify.
Folder Script Content cspAnalysis exhaustedModes.py H\(_2\)/air ignition: eigenvalues, M at three tolerance pairs, amplitudes subspaces.py CH\(_4\)/air ignition: fast/active/slow subspaces (calc_subspaces) indices.py Importance, participation and TSR indices at a single state indices-integral.py Time-integrated importance indices (index_norm = 'none') pointers.py CSP pointers JacobianSIM.py Eigenvalues of the SIM-constrained Jacobian (jacSIM) full_CSP_analysis.py Complete analysis stored in a TaggedDatabase and plotted with utils.save_CSP_plots dataImportExport export_import.py Writing a trajectory to file, reading it back and analysing it cspSolver cspsolver_const_p.py, cspsolver_const_v.py CSP solver at constant pressure and constant volume gscheme_const_p.py, gscheme_const_p_reuse.py G-Scheme, without and with basis reuse cspSimplify simp.py Skeletal mechanisms of GRI-3.0 for CH\(_4\)/air ignition simp_TSR.py The same, with the TSR target set, over several conditions tsrAnalysis TSR.py Chemical TSR during H\(_2\)/air ignition TSR_ext.py Extended TSR of a flamelet dataset

The reader is referred to [1]–[4], [6] for the theoretical details of the methods employed.

Analysing a reactor that shares the CanteraCSP object

In the examples, the CanteraCSP object is passed to a Cantera reactor, and the CSP quantities are queried on the same object while the reactor advances. With Cantera > 3.2, reactors clone the phase by default: create the reactor with utils.shared_reactor(ct.IdealGasConstPressureReactor, gas), or set the state explicitly on gas before each CSP query (e.g. gas.TPY = r.phase.TPY; r.thermo before Cantera 3.2). Setting the state also guarantees that the cached CSP kernel is updated (see CanteraCSP in Functions.py).

docs.title: Exhausted modes along a trajectory
docs.text:
This example analyses a set of thermochemical states stored in an external file called testdata.dat, containing \(N\) lines, each one being a full thermochemical state of the kind [t, T, P, Y_1, ..., Y_Ns]. Such a file is written by examples/dataImportExport/export_import.py. The kinetic mechanism is hydrogen.yaml, containing 9 species and 19 reversible reactions. The dataset is the time evolution of a stoichiometric H\(_2\)/air constant-pressure homogeneous reactor, with an initial temperature of 1000 K and a pressure of one atmosphere.

import numpy as np
import PyCSP.Functions as csp
import PyCSP.utils as utils
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

#import dataset
data = np.loadtxt('testdata.dat')
time = data[:,0]
Temp = data[:,1]
Pressure = data[:,2]
Y = data[:,3:]

#create an instance of the CanteraCSP class
gas = csp.CanteraCSP('hydrogen.yaml')

#set jacobiantype
gas.jacobiantype = 'full'

#set CSP tolerances
gas.rtol = 1.0e-2
gas.atol = 1.0e-8

evals = []
M = []

for step in range(len(time)):
    gas.constP = Pressure[step]
    state = np.append(Y[step],Temp[step])
    gas.set_stateYT(state)
    lam,R,L,f = gas.get_kernel()
    NofDM = gas.calc_exhausted_modes()
    evals.append(lam)
    M.append(NofDM)

evals = np.array(evals)
M = np.array(M)

#plot eigenvalues and lambda_M+1
evalM = utils.select_eval(evals,M)
logevals = np.clip(np.log10(1.0+np.abs(evals)),0,100)*np.sign(evals.real)
logevalM = np.clip(np.log10(1.0+np.abs(evalM)),0,100)*np.sign(evalM.real)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,4))
for idx in range(evals.shape[1]):
    ax.plot(time, logevals[:,idx], color='black', marker='.', markersize=5, linestyle='None')
ax.plot(time, logevalM, color='orange', marker='.', markersize=4, linestyle='None', label='lam(M+1) rtol e-2; atol e-8')
ax.set_xlabel('time (s)')
ax.set_ylabel('evals')
ax.set_ylim([-9, 6])
ax.set_xlim([0., 0.001])
ax.legend()
plt.show()

#plot exhausted modes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,4))
ax.plot(M, color='orange', label='rtol e-2; atol e-8')
ax.set_xlabel('# timestep')
ax.set_ylabel('M')
ax.set_ylim([0,10])
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Figure 2: Example outcomes. Left: eigenvalues (black) and M+1-th eigenvalue (orange). Right: number of exhausted modes.

docs.title: Fast, active and slow subspaces
docs.text:
calc_subspaces() returns both the number of exhausted modes \(M\) and the Head index \(H\), which partition the modes into fast \([0, M)\), active \([M, H)\) and slow \([H, N_v - N_{el})\) subspaces (see Theory). The script examples/cspAnalysis/subspaces.py computes them along the ignition of a stoichiometric CH\(_4\)/air mixture (GRI-3.0, 1000 K, 1 atm):

gas = csp.CanteraCSP('gri30.yaml')
...
while sim.time < 10:
    sim.step()
    states.append(r.thermo.state, t=sim.time)
    lam,R,L,f = gas.get_kernel()
    M, H = gas.calc_subspaces(rtolTail=1.0e-3,atolTail=1.0e-9,rtolHead=1.0e-3,atolHead=1.0e-9)

Figure 3: Eigenvalues (black, log-scaled) during CH4/air ignition, with the eigenvalues of mode M+1 (orange) and of mode H (blue) bounding the active subspace. Generated with PyCSP v1.5.0.

docs.title: Indices at a single state
docs.text:
examples/cspAnalysis/indices.py computes, at a given state, the CSP indices of all the reactions:

api, tpi, ifast, islow, species_type = gas.calc_CSPindices(API=True, TPI=True, Impo=True, species_type=True)
tsrapi = gas.calc_TSRindices(type='amplitude')
tsrtpi = gas.calc_TSRindices(type='timescale')

The indices are arrays of shape [N\(_v \times\) 2N\(_r\)] (modes for api and tpi, variables for ifast and islow), and the reaction names, forward and backward, are given by gas.reaction_names(). With gas.index_norm = 'none' the indices are not normalized and can be integrated in time (indices-integral.py).

docs.title: CSP simplify
docs.text:
This example shows how to generate a set of simplified kinetic mechanisms with the CSPsimplify class, based on a dataset produced with a detailed mechanism (examples/cspSimplify/simp.py).

import numpy as np
import cantera as ct
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import PyCSP.Functions as csp
import PyCSP.Simplify as simp
import PyCSP.utils as utils

#-------CREATE DATASET---------
#create gas from original mechanism file gri30.yaml
dtl_mech = csp.CanteraCSP('gri30.yaml')

#integrate ODE with detailed mech
T = 1000
P = ct.one_atm
states = utils.integrate_batch_constP(dtl_mech, T, P, 1.0, 'CH4', 'O2:1, N2:3.76', 1000)

dataset = np.concatenate((states.Y,states.T[:,np.newaxis],states.P[:,np.newaxis]),axis=1)
print('Dataset created, start processing...')

#coarsen dataset (to speed up)
dataset = dataset[::64]

#-------SIMPLIFY---------
#init simplifier
simplifier = simp.CSPsimplify(dtl_mech,dataset)

#simplifier settings
simplifier.targetset = {'CH4','O2','N2','HCO','H2O','CO2'}
simplifier.problemtype = 'constP'
simplifier.scaled = True
simplifier.csprtol = 1.0e-2
simplifier.cspatol = 1.0e-8

#process dataset
simplifier.process_dataset()

print('Done processing')

print('Start pruning...may take a while')
#loop over thresholds
thr = np.arange(0.01, 1, 0.01)

simp_mech = []
prev_species = dtl_mech.species_names
for i in range(len(thr)):
    species, reactions = simplifier.simplify_mechanism(thr[i])
    sk = csp.CanteraCSP(thermo='ideal-gas', kinetics='gas', species=species, reactions=reactions)
    if sk.species_names != prev_species:  #append only if different from previous one
        simp_mech.append(sk)
        prev_species = sk.species_names

nmech = len(simp_mech)
print('%i mechanisms found' % (nmech))

#-------RE-RUN---------
# Re-run the ignition problem with the simplified mechanisms
all_states_simp = []
for i in range(nmech):
    states_simp = utils.integrate_batch_constP(simp_mech[i], T, P, 1.0, 'CH4', 'O2:1, N2:3.76', 1000)
    all_states_simp.append(states_simp)

#-------ERRORS---------
dtl_idt = states.t[states.rhsT.argmax()]
simp_idt = np.array([all_states_simp[i].t[all_states_simp[i].rhsT.argmax()] for i in range(nmech)])
err_idt = abs((simp_idt-dtl_idt)/dtl_idt)*100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,4))
ax.plot([simp_mech[i].n_species for i in range(nmech)], err_idt, color='red', marker='.')
ax.set_xlabel('# of species')
ax.set_ylabel('ignition delay time relative Error [%]')
ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set_ylim([1e-3, 1e2])
plt.savefig('ign_delay_error.png', dpi=800, transparent=False)

A skeletal mechanism can be saved to file with Cantera's write_yaml() (or write_chemkin()) method, e.g. simp_mech[i].write_yaml('skeletal.yaml').

Figure 8: Example outcomes of the mechanism simplification.

Figure 8 shows the percent relative error on the ignition delay time versus the number of retained species. A significant improvement is given by the TSR kernel set, which replaces the user-specified target species set (see [3]). With the following settings:

simplifier.TSRtargetset = True
simplifier.TSRtol = 0.5
simplifier.targetset = {'N2'}

the previous example delivers the ignition delay relative errors shown in Figure 9. The manual addition of N\(_2\) to the TSR kernel set is needed to force the presence of N\(_2\) in the skeletal mechanisms.

Figure 9: Example outcomes of the mechanism simplification with TSR kernel set.

docs.title: CSP solver
docs.text:
This example shows how to integrate a constant-volume homogeneous reactor with the CSPsolver class (examples/cspSolver/cspsolver_const_v.py).

import numpy as np
import cantera as ct
import PyCSP.Functions as cspF
import PyCSP.Solver as cspS

#create an instance of the CanteraCSP class
gas = cspF.CanteraCSP('hydrogen.yaml')

#set the gas state using Cantera's methods (as an alternative to set_stateYT())
T = 1000
P = ct.one_atm
gas.TP = T, P
gas.set_equivalence_ratio(1.0, 'H2', 'O2:1, N2:3.76')

#push density
rho = gas.density
gas.constRho = rho

#initial condition
y0 = np.hstack((gas.Y,gas.T))
t0 = 0.0

t_end = 1e-2

#create an instance of CSPsolver
solver = cspS.CSPsolver(gas)
solver.set_integrator(cspRtol=1e-2,cspAtol=1e-8,factor=0.2,jacobiantype='full')
solver.set_initial_value(y0,t0)

states = ct.SolutionArray(gas, 1, extra={'t': [0.0], 'M': 0})

#integrate ODE with CSP solver
while solver.t < t_end:
    solver.integrate()
    states.append(gas.state, t=solver.t, M=solver.M)
    print('%10.3e %10.3f %10.3e %10.3e %10.3e %2i' % (solver.t, solver.y[-1], solver.dt, gas.P, gas.density, solver.M))

Figure 7: Example outcomes: temperature, OH, H, number of exhausted modes, density and pressure in a constant-volume reactor integrated with the CSP solver.

docs.title: G-Scheme
docs.text:
The G-Scheme integrates only the active modes, between the Tail (\(T\)) and Head (\(H\)) indices (examples/cspSolver/gscheme_const_p.py):

import PyCSP.GScheme as gsc

gas = cspF.CanteraCSP('gri30.yaml')
gas.TP = 1000, ct.one_atm
gas.set_equivalence_ratio(1.0, 'CH4', 'O2:1, N2:3.76')
gas.constP = ct.one_atm

y0 = np.hstack((gas.Y,gas.T))
solver = gsc.GScheme(gas)
solver.set_integrator(cspRtolTail=1e-3,cspAtolTail=1e-9,cspRtolHead=1e-4,cspAtolHead=1e-10,
                      factor=0.25,jacobiantype='full')
solver.set_initial_value(y0,0.0)

states = ct.SolutionArray(gas, 1, extra={'t': [0.0], 'Tail': 0, 'Head': 0, 'dt': [0.0]})
while solver.t < 2.0:
    solver.integrate()
    states.append(gas.state, t=solver.t, Tail=solver.T, Head=solver.H, dt=solver.dt)

solver.profiling()

With solver.reuse = True the CSP basis is reused while the Jacobian diagonal changes by less than solver.reuseThr (gscheme_const_p_reuse.py).

docs.title: Full CSP analysis and plots
docs.text:
The script examples/cspAnalysis/full_CSP_analysis.py runs a complete CSP analysis of the H\(_2\)/air constant-pressure ignition. It stores the results in a utils.TaggedDatabase and generates all the plots with utils.save_CSP_plots. This workflow is new in the v1.5 documentation.

import numpy as np
import PyCSP.Functions as csp
import PyCSP.utils as utils

gas = csp.CanteraCSP('hydrogen.yaml')
P = 101325.0
states = utils.integrate_batch_constP(gas, 1000.0, P, 1.0, 'H2', 'O2:1, N2:3.76', 1e-3)

db = utils.TaggedDatabase()
for step in range(len(states.t)):
    stateYT = np.append(states.Y[step], states.T[step])
    gas.constP = P
    gas.jacobiantype = 'full'
    gas.set_stateYT(stateYT)

    lam, R, L, f = gas.get_kernel()
    frozen = csp.detectFrozenModes(gas.nv-gas.n_elements, stateYT, R, L,
                                   gas.generalized_Stoich_matrix, gas.R_vector, 1e-4, 1e-12)
    M = gas.calc_exhausted_modes()
    api, tpi, ifast, islow, species_type = gas.calc_CSPindices(API=True, Impo=True, species_type=True)

    db.store(time=states.t[step], state=stateYT, evals=lam, Revec=R, Levec=L, fvec=f,
             M=M, frozen=frozen, tsr=gas.calc_TSR(), API=api, Ifast=ifast, Islow=islow,
             species_type=species_type, Pointers=csp.CSP_pointers(R, L),
             tsrApi=gas.calc_TSRindices(type='amplitude'),
             tsrTpi=gas.calc_TSRindices(type='timescale'))

db.to_arrays()
utils.save_CSP_plots(db, gas, output_folder='CSP_Plots', threshold=0.2,
                     species_threshold=1e-4, xlim=(0, 0.001), xlabel='time [s]')

The tags recognized by save_CSP_plots are listed in the utils.py page. Some of the plots generated by the script are shown below.

Figure 4: Eigenvalues (black), eigenvalue of mode M+1 (orange) and TSR (green), together with temperature (grey). Generated with PyCSP v1.5.0.

Figure 5: Map of the slow, exhausted and frozen modes during the ignition. Generated with PyCSP v1.5.0.

Figure 6: Map of the fast and slow species, from the CSP pointers. Generated with PyCSP v1.5.0.

docs.title: Chemical TSR
docs.text:
This example shows how to compute the TSR of data points produced in a homogeneous reactor auto-ignition (examples/tsrAnalysis/TSR.py).

import numpy as np
import cantera as ct
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import PyCSP.Functions as csp
import PyCSP.utils as utils

#create gas from original mechanism file hydrogen.yaml
gas = csp.CanteraCSP('hydrogen.yaml')

#set the gas state
T = 1000
P = ct.one_atm
gas.TP = T, P
gas.set_equivalence_ratio(1.0, 'H2', 'O2:1, N2:3.76')
gas.constP = P
gas.jacobiantype = 'full'

#integrate ODE
r = utils.shared_reactor(ct.IdealGasConstPressureReactor, gas)
sim = ct.ReactorNet([r])
states = ct.SolutionArray(gas, extra=['t'])

evals = []
M = []
tsr = []

while sim.time < 10:
    sim.step()
    states.append(gas.state, t=sim.time)
    lam,R,L,f = gas.get_kernel()
    omegatau, NofDM = gas.calc_TSR(getM=True,rtol=1.0e-3,atol=1.0e-10)
    evals.append(lam)
    M.append(NofDM)
    tsr.append(omegatau)

evals = np.array(evals)
M = np.array(M)
tsr = np.array(tsr)

#plot eigenvalues, lambda_M+1 and TSR
evalM = utils.select_eval(evals,M)
logevals = np.clip(np.log10(1.0+np.abs(evals.real)),0,100)*np.sign(evals.real)
logevalM = np.clip(np.log10(1.0+np.abs(evalM.real)),0,100)*np.sign(evalM.real)
logTSR = np.clip(np.log10(1.0+np.abs(tsr)),0,100)*np.sign(tsr)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,4))
for idx in range(evals.shape[1]):
    ax.plot(states.t, logevals[:,idx], color='black', marker='.', markersize=5, linestyle='None')
ax.plot(states.t, logevalM, color='orange', marker='.', markersize=4, linestyle='None', label='lam(M+1)')
ax.plot(states.t, logTSR, color='green', marker='.', markersize=2, linestyle='None', label='TSR')
ax.set_xlabel('time (s)')
ax.set_ylabel('evals')
ax.set_ylim([-9, 6])
ax.set_xlim([0., 0.001])
ax.legend()
plt.savefig('TSR.png', dpi=500, transparent=False)

Figure 10: Example outcomes of the TSR analysis.

Figure 10 shows the TSR compared to the system's eigenvalues.

docs.title: Extended TSR
docs.text:
This example shows how to perform an extended TSR analysis of pre-computed thermochemical data stored in two external files:

  • flamelet_state.dat contains \(N\) lines, each one being a full thermochemical state of the kind [time, counter, Z, P, T, Y_1, ..., Y_Ns];
  • flamelet_rhsDiff.dat contains the diffusive terms, in the form [time, counter, Z, diff-T, diff-Y_1, ..., diff-Y_Ns].

This analysis can be performed supplying either the diffusive terms, the convective terms, or both simultaneously. The kinetic mechanism is chaos12.yaml, containing 12 species and 33 reversible reactions. The dataset and the results are described in [4] (examples/tsrAnalysis/TSR_ext.py).

import numpy as np
import PyCSP.Functions as csp

#create gas from original mechanism file chaos12.yaml
gas = csp.CanteraCSP('chaos12.yaml')

#-------IMPORT DATA---------
#read data from file
state = np.loadtxt('flamelet_state.dat')
time = state[:,0]
counter = state[:,1]
zeta = state[:,2]
Pressure = state[:,3]
Temp = state[:,4]
Y = state[:,5:]

rhsD = np.loadtxt('flamelet_rhsDiff.dat')
diffTemp = rhsD[:,3]
diffY = rhsD[:,4:]

#set jacobiantype
gas.jacobiantype = 'full'

evals = []
M = []
tsr = []
Mext = []
tsrext = []

print('Analyzing %i data points, may take a while...' %len(state))

for step in range(time.shape[0]):
    gas.constP = Pressure[step]
    stateYT = np.append(Y[step],Temp[step])
    rhsdiffYT = np.append(diffY[step],diffTemp[step])
    gas.set_stateYT(stateYT)
    lam,R,L,f = gas.get_kernel()
    omegatau, NofDM = gas.calc_TSR(getM=True)
    omegatauext, NofDMext = gas.calc_extended_TSR(getMext=True,diff=rhsdiffYT)

    evals.append(lam)
    M.append(NofDM)
    tsr.append(omegatau)
    Mext.append(NofDMext)
    tsrext.append(omegatauext)

evals = np.array(evals)
Mext = np.array(Mext)
tsrext = np.array(tsrext)
M = np.array(M)
tsr = np.array(tsr)

Figure 11 shows the contour plots of the chemical and extended TSR.

Figure 11: Example outcomes. Left: contour plot of the chemical TSR. Right: contour plot of the extended TSR.

The amplitude participation indices (API) to the extended TSR can be obtained as:

omegatauext, api = gas.calc_extended_TSRindices(diff=rhsdiffYT, getTSRext=True)

The indices refer to the 2N\(_r\) reactions followed by the N\(_v\) convective and the N\(_v\) diffusive terms. Figure 12 shows the TSR-API in a slice of the field.

Figure 12: Example outcomes. Amplitude Participation Indices to the extended TSR.

docs.title: CSP and TSR analysis
docs.text: This page collects the definitions of the quantities computed by the CSP and TSR analysis tools of PyCSP, written as they are implemented. The algorithms built on them are described in the mechanism simplification and CSP solver and G-Scheme pages. The reader is referred to [1]–[7] for the theoretical background of the methods.

docs.title: Governing equations
docs.text:
PyCSP considers a homogeneous, adiabatic reacting mixture of \(N_s\) species and \(N_r\) reversible reactions. The state vector collects the species mass fractions and the temperature,

\[ \mathbf{y} = [\,Y_1, \dots, Y_{N_s}, T\,]^T, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt} = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y}), \]

with \(N_v = N_s + 1\) variables. Forward and backward directions of each reaction are treated as separate processes, so that there are \(2N_r\) rates of progress \(r^k\) [kmol/m\(^3\)/s] and the net molar production rate of species \(i\) is \(\dot{\omega}_i = \sum_{k=1}^{2N_r} \nu_{ik} r^k\). Here \(\nu_{ik}\) is the net stoichiometric coefficient of species \(i\) in process \(k\). It is positive for products, and its sign is reversed for the backward direction.

docs.title: Constant pressure (problemtype = 'const_p')
docs.text:
\[ g_i = \frac{W_i}{\rho}\,\dot{\omega}_i \quad (i = 1,\dots,N_s), \qquad g_T = -\frac{1}{c_p} \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} h_i\, g_i , \]

where \(W_i\) is the molecular weight of species \(i\), \(\rho\) the mixture density, \(c_p\) the mixture specific heat at constant pressure [J/kg/K] and \(h_i = H_i/W_i\) the specific enthalpy of species \(i\) [J/kg] (with \(H_i\) the molar enthalpy).

docs.title: Constant volume (problemtype = 'const_v')
docs.text:
\[ g_i = \frac{W_i}{\rho}\,\dot{\omega}_i , \qquad g_T = -\frac{1}{c_v} \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} u_i\, g_i = -\frac{1}{c_v} \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} h_i\, g_i + \frac{R\,T}{c_v} \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} \frac{g_i}{W_i}, \]

where \(c_v\) is the mixture specific heat at constant volume, \(u_i = h_i - RT/W_i\) the specific internal energy of species \(i\) and \(R\) the universal gas constant.

docs.title: Generalized stoichiometric matrix
docs.text:
The source term is written as the sum of the contributions of the \(2N_r\) processes, \(\mathbf{g} = \mathcal{S}\,\mathbf{r} = \sum_k \mathcal{S}_k\, r^k\), where \(\mathcal{S}_k\) is the \(k\)-th column of the generalized stoichiometric matrix \(\mathcal{S}\) [\(N_v imes 2N_r\)]:

\[ \mathcal{S}_{i,k} = rac{W_i}{ ho}\, u_{ik} \qquad i = 1,\dots,N_s , \] \[ ext{const. pressure:}\quad \mathcal{S}_{T,k} = - rac{1}{ ho\, c_p} \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} u_{ik}\, H_i , \] \[ ext{const. volume:}\quad \mathcal{S}_{T,k} = - rac{1}{ ho\, c_v} \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} u_{ik}\, (H_i - R\,T) . \]

docs.title: Jacobian
docs.text:
The Jacobian \(\mathbf{J} = \partial \mathbf{g}/\partial \mathbf{y}\) is evaluated by forward finite differences. Each mass fraction \(Y_j\) is perturbed without renormalizing the others, at constant temperature. Temperature is perturbed at constant composition. In both cases the thermodynamic constraint of the problem is held fixed:

\[ J_{ij} = \left.\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial Y_j}\right|_{T,\,P\ \text{or}\ \rho}, \qquad J_{i,T} = \left.\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial T}\right|_{Y,\,P\ \text{or}\ \rho}, \]

with steps \(\delta Y_j = \max(\sqrt{\epsilon}\,|Y_j|,\,10^{-8})\) and \(\delta T = \max(\sqrt{\epsilon}\,T,\,10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K})\), \(\epsilon\) being the machine precision.

Three Jacobian types are available (attribute jacobiantype of CanteraCSP):

full The \(N_v \times N_v\) Jacobian of \((Y_1,\dots,Y_{N_s},T)\). kinetic The \(N_s \times N_s\) species block \(\mathbf{J}_{YY}\), temperature being frozen. constrained

The \(N_s \times N_s\) Jacobian of the species equations on the manifold of constant enthalpy (constant pressure) or constant internal energy (constant volume), where temperature is a function of the composition. Differentiating \(\sum_i Y_i e_i(T) = \text{const}\) gives \(\partial T/\partial Y_j = -e_j/c\), hence

\[ \mathbf{J}^{c} = \mathbf{J}_{YY} - \mathbf{J}_{YT}\, \frac{\mathbf{e}^T}{c}, \qquad e_j = h_j,\ c = c_p \ \ \text{(const. pressure)}, \qquad e_j = u_j,\ c = c_v \ \ \text{(const. volume)}. \]

The correction term is returned by jacThermal().

The contribution of process \(k\) to the Jacobian is \(\mathbf{J}_k = \partial(\mathcal{S}_k r^k)/\partial \mathbf{y}\), so that \(\mathbf{J} = \sum_{k=1}^{2N_r} \mathbf{J}_k\) (method jac_contribution(), available for the full and kinetic types).

docs.title: CSP kernel
docs.text:
The CSP basis is the eigenvector basis of the Jacobian (zeroth-order CSP basis):

  • Eigenvalues. The eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) are sorted by decreasing modulus. The last \(N_{el}\) eigenvalues, with \(N_{el}\) the number of chemical elements, correspond to the elemental conservation laws and are set exactly to zero.
  • Basis vectors. The right eigenvectors \(\mathbf{a}_i\) are the rows of Revec (\(\mathbf{A}\)). The dual basis vectors \(\mathbf{b}^i\) are the rows of Levec (\(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A}^{-T}\) in matrix form, such that \(\mathbf{b}^i\cdot\mathbf{a}_j = \delta^i_j\)).
  • Complex-conjugate pairs. A complex-conjugate pair \(\lambda = \alpha \pm i\beta\) with eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}, \bar{\mathbf{v}}\) is represented by the real vectors \(\mathbf{a}_i = \mathrm{Re}\,\mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{a}_{i+1} = \mathrm{Im}\,\mathbf{v}\).
  • Mode amplitudes. \(f^i = \mathbf{b}^i \cdot \mathbf{g}\), so that \(\mathbf{g} = \sum_i \mathbf{a}_i f^i\). The sign of each pair \((\mathbf{a}_i, \mathbf{b}^i)\) is chosen such that \(f^i \ge 0\).
  • Timescales. \(\tau_i = 1/|\lambda_i|\).

Note

The sign of a mode whose amplitude is (numerically) zero, e.g. an exhausted mode, is arbitrary. Quantities that depend on the sign of \(\mathbf{a}_i\) or \(\mathbf{b}^i\) separately, such as the amplitude participation indices of that mode, may flip sign from one state to the next.

docs.title: Exhausted modes
docs.text:
The number \(M\) of exhausted (fast) modes is the largest \(m\) such that, for all \(m' \le m\), the cumulative contribution of the first \(m'\) modes over the timescale of the next mode is below the error tolerance:

\[ \left| \sum_{r=1}^{m'} \mathbf{a}_r\, f^r\, \frac{e^{\lambda_r \tau_{r+1}} - 1}{\lambda_r} \right|_j < \mathrm{rtol}\, |y_j| + \mathrm{atol} \qquad \forall\, j = 1,\dots,N_v , \]

where \(\lambda_r\) denotes the real part of the eigenvalue. In other words, a mode is fast if it has relaxed close enough to its local quasi-equilibrium that its remaining drift, integrated over the first active timescale, no longer matters at the prescribed accuracy. \(M\) never separates the two members of a complex-conjugate pair, and at least one non-conserved mode is left active. The tolerances are the attributes rtol and atol of CanteraCSP (or keyword arguments of the calc_* methods).

docs.title: Slow modes
docs.text:
The Head index \(H\) separates the active modes \([M, H)\) from the slow ones \([H, N_v - N_{el})\), following the G-Scheme [6]. Scanning the non-conserved modes backwards from the slowest one, a mode \(j\) is slow if the cumulative second order contribution of the slower modes (slow/dormant modes are quasi-linear in the active timeframe) stays below the tolerance over the timescale \(\Delta t\):

\[ \left| \sum_{r \ge j} \tfrac{1}{2}\,\Delta t^2\, |\lambda_r|\, \mathbf{a}_r\, f^r \right|_j < \mathrm{rtol}_H\, |y_j| + \mathrm{atol}_H . \]

In calc_subspaces(), \(\Delta t = \tau_{M+1}\); in the G-Scheme integrator, \(\Delta t\) is the integration time step.

docs.title: Tangential Stretching Rate
docs.text:
The TSR [4] is a weighted average of the eigenvalues:

\[ \omega_\tau = \sum_{i} W^i\, \mathrm{sgn}(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i)\, |\lambda_i|, \qquad W^i = \frac{(f^i/\|\mathbf{g}\|)^2}{\sum_j (f^j/\|\mathbf{g}\|)^2} . \]
  • Excluded modes. The weights of the \(M\) exhausted modes and of the conserved modes (zero eigenvalue) are set to zero, so that the sum runs over the active and slow modes only.
  • Complex pairs. For a complex pair, both amplitudes are replaced by \(\sqrt{(f^i)^2 + (f^{i+1})^2}\).
  • Extended TSR. For reaction-diffusion-convection systems [4], \(\mathbf{g}\) is replaced by \(\mathbf{g} + \mathbf{L}\), where \(\mathbf{L}\) is the sum of the transport terms (diffusion and/or convection, supplied by the user in the same units as \(\mathbf{g}\)). The amplitudes become \(h^i = \mathbf{b}^i\cdot(\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{L})\), and \(M\) is recomputed with these amplitudes (\(M_{ext}\)).

docs.title: CSP indices
docs.text: All the indices are normalized, unless index_norm = 'none', by the sum of the absolute values of the contributions, so that their absolute values sum to one. The optional norm_cut (new in v1.5) sets to zero, instead of normalizing, the indices whose sum of absolute contributions is smaller than the cut.

docs.title: Amplitude participation index (API)
docs.text:
The participation of process \(k\) to the amplitude of mode \(i\) [1]:

\[ P^i_k = \frac{\mathbf{b}^i\cdot\mathcal{S}_k\, r^k}{\sum_{k'=1}^{2N_r} |\mathbf{b}^i\cdot\mathcal{S}_{k'}\, r^{k'}|} . \]

For an exhausted mode, the processes with large \(|P^i_k|\) are the ones in equilibrium.

docs.title: Timescale participation index (TPI)
docs.text:
The participation of process \(k\) to the eigenvalue (hence the timescale) of mode \(i\) [1]. From \(\lambda_i = \mathbf{b}^i\cdot\mathbf{J}\,\mathbf{a}_i = \sum_k c^k_i\), with \(c^k_i = \mathbf{b}^i\cdot\mathbf{J}_k\,\mathbf{a}_i\):

\[ J^i_k = \frac{c^k_i}{\sum_{k'} |c^{k'}_i|} . \]

For a complex-conjugate pair the index decomposes \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i\), using \(c^k_i = \tfrac12\left(\mathbf{b}^i\cdot\mathbf{J}_k\,\mathbf{a}_i + \mathbf{b}^{i+1}\cdot\mathbf{J}_k\,\mathbf{a}_{i+1}\right)\).

docs.title: Importance indices
docs.text:
The fast and slow importance indices of process \(k\) to variable \(j\) [1] measure the contribution of process \(k\) to the fast and slow projections of \(\mathbf{g}\):

\[ I^{j}_{k,\text{fast}} = \frac{\left(\mathbf{Q}_{\text{fast}}\,\mathcal{S}_k\, r^k\right)_j}{\sum_{k'} \left|\left(\mathbf{Q}_{\text{fast}}\,\mathcal{S}_{k'}\, r^{k'}\right)_j\right|}, \qquad \mathbf{Q}_{\text{fast}} = \sum_{r=1}^{M} \mathbf{a}_r \mathbf{b}^r , \]

and similarly for \(I^{j}_{k,\text{slow}}\), with \(\mathbf{Q}_{\text{slow}} = \sum_{r > M} \mathbf{a}_r \mathbf{b}^r\).

docs.title: TSR participation indices
docs.text:
The participation of mode \(i\) to the TSR, as implemented, is

\[ P^{\omega_\tau}_i = \frac{W^i\,|\lambda_i|}{\sum_j W^j\,|\lambda_j|} , \]

and the participation of process \(k\) to the TSR combines it with the API (TSR-API) or the TPI (TSR-TPI) of each mode [4]:

\[ P^{\omega_\tau}_k = \sum_i |P^{\omega_\tau}_i|\, P^i_k \quad \text{(TSR-API)}, \qquad \sum_i |P^{\omega_\tau}_i|\, J^i_k \quad \text{(TSR-TPI)}, \]

normalized by the sum of absolute values.

docs.title: CSP pointers and species classification
docs.text:
The CSP pointer of mode \(m\) to variable \(j\) is the diagonal element \((\mathbf{a}_m \mathbf{b}^m)_{jj}\), following Lam and Goussis. PyCSP classifies the species with the following steps:

  1. Sum the pointers of the \(M\) exhausted modes, \(\hat{Q}_{jj} = \sum_{m=1}^{M} (\mathbf{a}_m \mathbf{b}^m)_{jj}\).
  2. Label as fast the \(M\) variables with the largest \(\hat{Q}_{jj}\). Temperature is always labelled slow.
  3. Label all other species slow.
  4. Optionally (classify_traces = True), label as trace the species with \(Y_j < 10^{-20}\) and non-positive source term.

docs.title: SIM-constrained Jacobian
docs.text: jacSIM() returns the Jacobian of the slow dynamics constrained to the slow invariant manifold (SIM) defined by the \(M\) exhausted modes, expressed in terms of a set of major variables. The theoretical details can be found in [5].

docs.title: Mechanism simplification
docs.text: The class CSPsimplify generates skeletal kinetic mechanisms from a detailed one, following the CSP-based algorithm of [3]. The algorithm uses the CSP importance indices and the species classification, computed on a dataset of thermochemical states that is representative of the application, e.g. the ignition trajectory of a homogeneous reactor. This page describes the algorithm as implemented.

docs.title: Input data
docs.text:
The dataset is a 2D array, each row being a thermochemical state \([\,Y_1, \dots, Y_{N_s}, T, P\,]\) computed with the detailed mechanism. process_dataset() analyses each state \(n\) of the dataset, with the full Jacobian and the CSP tolerances csprtol, cspatol. It stores:

  • the absolute values of the fast and slow importance indices, \(|I^{j}_{k,\text{fast}}|\) and \(|I^{j}_{k,\text{slow}}|\), of each process \(k\) (forward and backward reactions) to each variable \(j\) (species and temperature);
  • the classification of each species as fast, slow or trace;
  • if the TSR target set is active, the absolute values of the TSR amplitude participation indices \(|P^{\omega_\tau}_k|\).

With problemtype = 'constP' the indices are computed at the pressure of each state. With 'constRho' they are computed at the density of each state.

docs.title: Active species of one state
docs.text:
Given a threshold \(\theta \in [0, 1]\), the set of active species \(\mathcal{A}_n\) of state \(n\) is built iteratively. It starts from the target set \(\mathcal{T}\) of species chosen by the user (targetset).

  1. Relevant reactions. For each active species \(j\), the processes that are relevant to its evolution are selected with the importance indices of the subspace that governs that species:

    • if \(j\) is a slow species, the processes \(k\) with \(|I^{j}_{k,\text{slow}}| \ge \theta\, \max_{k'} |I^{j}_{k',\text{slow}}|\);
    • if \(j\) is a fast species, the processes \(k\) with \(|I^{j}_{k,\text{fast}}| \ge \theta\, \max_{k'} |I^{j}_{k',\text{fast}}|\).

    The processes relevant to temperature are always selected, with its slow importance indices. With scaled = False, the criterion is \(|I| \ge \theta\) instead of being relative to the maximum.

  2. New species. All the species involved (as reactants or products) in the selected reactions become active.

  3. Trace species. The species classified as trace are removed from the active set.
  4. Iteration. Steps 1–3 are repeated until the active set no longer changes.

Finally, the target species are added back to \(\mathcal{A}_n\), so that target species removed as trace species (e.g. inert species) are retained.

docs.title: Skeletal mechanism
docs.text:
The species of the skeletal mechanism are the union of the active sets over the dataset, \(\mathcal{A} = \bigcup_n \mathcal{A}_n\). Its reactions are all the reactions of the detailed mechanism whose reactants and products all belong to \(\mathcal{A}\).

simplify_mechanism(threshold) returns these species and reactions. A small threshold retains more reactions per species, and hence produces larger and more accurate mechanisms. Scanning the threshold between 0 and 1 produces a family of skeletal mechanisms of decreasing size (see the example).

docs.title: TSR target set
docs.text:
The choice of the target set affects the result. With TSRtargetset = True, each state receives its own additional target species, chosen by the TSR [3]. These are the species involved in the processes that contribute the most to the TSR, which in turn identifies the most energetic timescale of the system:

  1. The processes are sorted by decreasing \(|P^{\omega_\tau}_k|\).
  2. The smallest leading group whose cumulative participation exceeds TSRtol is selected. The higher TSRtol, the more processes and species are included.
  3. The reactants and products of the selected reactions are added to the target set of that state.

The user-defined targetset may then be empty, or contain only the species that must be retained in any case, e.g. N\(_2\).

docs.title: Normalization cut
docs.text: With norm_cut (new in v1.5), the importance and TSR indices whose sum of absolute contributions is smaller than the cut are set to zero instead of being normalized. For example, the indices of a variable whose rate of change is negligible no longer select any reaction. See calc_CSPindices in Functions.py.

docs.title: Merging mechanisms
docs.text: merge_mechanisms(gasdtl, species1, species2) returns the skeletal mechanism containing the union of the species of two skeletal mechanisms derived from the same detailed mechanism, e.g. mechanisms generated for different operating conditions. The reactions are recovered from the detailed mechanism with the same criterion as above.

docs.title: CSP solver and G-Scheme
docs.text:
PyCSP includes two explicit integrators for the stiff chemical system \(d\mathbf{y}/dt = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y})\). They use the CSP decomposition to remove the fast timescales from the integration:

  • the CSP solver integrates all the non-exhausted modes. Works in physical coordinates;
  • the G-Scheme [6] integrates only the active modes. Works in intrinsic coordinates.

In both cases the time step is set by the fastest retained mode rather than by the fastest mode of the system. This page describes the algorithms as implemented. The notation (basis vectors \(\mathbf{a}_r\), \(\mathbf{b}^r\), amplitudes \(f^r\), eigenvalues \(\lambda_r\), timescales \(\tau_r\)) is that of the CSP and TSR analysis page, with modes numbered \(r = 1, \dots, N_v\) in order of decreasing \(|\lambda_r|\); only the real part of \(\lambda_r\) enters the corrections below.

docs.title: Subspaces
docs.text:
Each solver step partitions the modes into:

Subspace Modes Treatment fast (exhausted) \(r = 1,\dots,M\) algebraic constraint \(f^r \approx 0\), enforced by a correction active \(r = M+1,\dots,H\) integrated in time slow (G-Scheme only) \(r = H+1,\dots,N_v-N_{el}\) correction over the time step conserved \(r = N_v-N_{el}+1,\dots,N_v\) not evolving

\(M\) (called Tail, \(T\), in the G-Scheme) and \(H\) (Head) are computed with the criteria of the analysis page. The CSP solver has no slow subspace: all the non-exhausted modes are integrated.

docs.title: Time step
docs.text:
The time step lies between the timescale of the fastest retained mode and that of the fastest exhausted mode:

\[ \Delta t = \tau_M + \gamma\,(\tau_{M+1} - \tau_M) \quad (M > 0), \qquad \Delta t = \gamma\,\tau_1 \quad (M = 0), \]

with \(\gamma\) = factor (default 0.2). The step may grow by at most 50% with respect to the previous one.

docs.title: Radical (tail) correction
docs.text:
The exhausted modes have decayed, but their residual amplitude would drive the state away from the slow manifold. The correction removes the displacement that these modes would produce if they relaxed exponentially over the timescale of the first non-exhausted mode, \(\tau_{M+1} = 1/|\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{M+1}|\):

\[ \mathbf{y} \leftarrow \mathbf{y} - \sum_{r=1}^{M} \mathbf{a}_r\, f^r\, \frac{1 - e^{\lambda_r \tau_{M+1}}}{\lambda_r} . \]

For a fast dissipative mode, \(\lambda_r \tau_{M+1} \ll -1\), so the correction reduces to the classical radical correction \(\mathbf{y} \leftarrow \mathbf{y} - \sum_{r} \mathbf{a}_r f^r/\lambda_r\).

docs.title: CSP solver
docs.text:
One step of CSPsolver.integrate(), from \(\mathbf{y}_n\):

  1. Basis. Compute the CSP basis at \(\mathbf{y}_n\).
  2. Radical correction. Apply the radical correction with the current \(M\), giving \(\mathbf{y}^\ast\).
  3. Exhausted modes. Update \(M\) at \(\mathbf{y}^\ast\), with the basis of step 1 and the tolerances csprtol, cspatol, and compute \(\Delta t\).

  4. Integration. Integrate the projected system with a fourth-order Runge–Kutta step:

    \[ \frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt} = \mathbf{Q}_s\, \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y}), \qquad \mathbf{Q}_s = \mathbf{I} - \sum_{r=1}^{M} \mathbf{a}_r \mathbf{b}^r . \]

    The projector \(\mathbf{Q}_s\) removes the fast components of the source term.

  5. Second correction. Apply the radical correction again, with the amplitudes evaluated at the new state, giving \(\mathbf{y}_{n+1}\); \(t_{n+1} = t_n + \Delta t\).

docs.title: G-Scheme
docs.text:
One step of GScheme.integrate(), from \(\mathbf{y}_n\):

  1. Basis. Compute the CSP basis at \(\mathbf{y}_n\), or reuse the previous one (see Basis reuse).
  2. Tail correction. Apply the tail correction (the radical correction above) with the current \(T\).
  3. Tail and time step. Update \(T\) with csprtolT, cspatolT, and compute \(\Delta t\).
  4. Head. Update \(H\) with csprtolH, cspatolH, over the horizon \(\Delta t\).

  5. Active integration. Integrate the active dynamics only, in the coordinates \(\mathbf{\xi}\) of the active subspace:

    \[ \mathbf{y}(t) = \mathbf{y}_n + \sum_{r=T+1}^{H} \mathbf{a}_r\, \xi^r(t), \qquad \frac{d\xi^r}{dt} = \mathbf{b}^r \cdot \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y}), \qquad \mathbf{\xi}(t_n) = 0, \]

    with a fourth-order Runge–Kutta step. The dimension of this system is \(H - T\), usually much smaller than \(N_v\).

  6. Head correction. Account for the slow modes over the step, with their amplitudes evaluated at the new state. Each slow mode contributes \(\mathbf{a}_r f^r (e^{\lambda_r \Delta t} - 1)/\lambda_r\), expanded for small \(\lambda_r \Delta t\):

    \[ \mathbf{y} \leftarrow \mathbf{y} + \sum_{r=H+1}^{N_v - N_{el}} \mathbf{a}_r\, f^r\, \Delta t \left(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\lambda_r \Delta t\right) . \]

  7. Tail correction. Apply the tail correction again, giving \(\mathbf{y}_{n+1}\); \(t_{n+1} = t_n + \Delta t\).

docs.title: Basis reuse
docs.text:
The basis computation (Jacobian and eigen-decomposition) is the most expensive part of a step. With reuse = True, the basis of the previous step is kept, and only the amplitudes are recomputed, as long as the Jacobian changes little. The change is measured on the inexpensive approximation of the Jacobian diagonal, \(\mathbf{d}\) (attribute jacobian_diagonal):

\[ u = \left\| \left( rac{d_j^{\,new} - d_j^{\,old}}{d_j^{\,new}} ight)_{j=1,\dots,N_s} ight\|_2 , \]

where entries with \(|d_j^{\,new}| \le 10^{-20}\) are skipped. The basis is recomputed during the first three steps, when \( u\) exceeds reuseThr, or after 250 consecutive reuses. The attributes normJac (\( u\)), basisStatus, skipBasis and updateBasis track the reuse.
